820.title: The Gita begins in grief
820.hook: the Gita opens with a general's briefing and a wall of conches, and its first chapter ends with Arjuna sitting down in grief.
820.carry: the gita's first yoga is honest grief
820.tomorrow: The self that is never killed
820.howItsDone: In the traditionally recited Gita, each chapter closes with a title naming it a yoga; the first is Arjuna Vishada Yoga, the yoga of Arjuna's despair, and the conches it names, like Krishna's Panchajanya, are familiar from pictures of Krishna and Arjuna in the chariot.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Bhishma Parva opened in a dark room: a blind king who refused to watch the war, and Sanjaya, who told him all of it. Your line: shravana: hearing holy words is devotion.
screen: `A BLIND KING WON'T WATCH.` · `SANJAYA TELLS IT ALL.`

segments.voice: Ask someone how the Bhagavad Gita begins, and they may tell you about Krishna's teaching. But after the old king's question, the first real speech belongs to Duryodhana, briefing his old teacher Drona. It sounds like a general's report. Today: the noise before the silence.
screen: `WHO SPEAKS FIRST?` → `DURYODHANA, TO HIS TEACHER` → `THE NOISE BEFORE THE SILENCE`

segments.voice: Duryodhana stands before Drona and points across the field. Look at the Pandava army, he says, arrayed by your own student. Then he tells everyone to guard Bhishma. Bhishma doesn't answer in words. To cheer him, the old grandsire roars like a lion and blows his conch, and the field erupts. Krishna blows his conch, Panchajanya. Arjuna blows his, Devadatta. The Gita says the sound made earth and sky resound. Then Arjuna asks Krishna to drive the chariot out between the armies, so he can see who he's about to fight. Krishna sets it down in front of Bhishma and Drona. And Arjuna looks. Grandfathers. Teachers. Uncles. Brothers. Sons. Friends. His limbs give way. His bow, Gandiva, slips from his hand, and he sits down in the chariot, overwhelmed with grief. Here's the surprising part. In the Gita as it's traditionally recited, every chapter closes with a title, and every title calls that chapter a yoga, a path to God. This one is called Arjuna Vishada Yoga: the yoga of Arjuna's despair. The hero is in tears, and the tradition still counts it as a path. Many teachers read it this way: honest grief is the doorway, because a man who thinks he has every answer never asks for a teacher. Krishna doesn't start teaching here. He waits, and in the next chapter, when Arjuna admits he is lost and asks to be taught, the Gita's great teaching begins. That's one reason so many Hindus turn to the Gita in their hardest weeks: a loss, a family fight, a week that crushes you. It doesn't begin with a hero who has it together. It begins with someone who can't go on, and calls that the first step.
screen: `DURYODHANA BRIEFS, BHISHMA ROARS` · `ARJUNA LOOKS, AND SITS DOWN` · `ARJUNA VISHADA YOGA` · then, large: `HONEST GRIEF, THE FIRST STEP`

segments.voice: Sit the way Arjuna sat, set down in the chariot. Breathing in, name honestly one thing that feels too heavy right now; you don't have to fix it. Breathing out, set it down beside you, the way he set down his bow. Many Hindus bring a heavy heart to Krishna just like this, before asking for anything. If you pray, tell God plainly what's heavy. If you don't, simply let it be named.
Bhishma Parva. The book named for the grandsire, whose conch started the noise that ends in Arjuna's grief, and the Gita's first yoga.
Your line: the Gita's first yoga is honest grief. All those conches, and the teaching begins with a bow set down. Until tomorrow.

821.title: The self that is never killed
821.hook: a warrior asks his charioteer to teach him, and the first lesson is about what in us can never die.
821.carry: the atman is never born and never dies
821.howItsDone: The Gita's second chapter, with its verses on the self that is never born and never dies, is often read or recited when someone dies, at the bedside or at the prayer gathering afterward.

segments.voice: Yesterday the conches roared and Arjuna sat down in his chariot. Your line: the Gita's first yoga is honest grief.

A chariot stands alone in the open ground, with an army on either side, waiting. The warrior in it is a great archer, and he has just put his bow down. The man holding the reins is his cousin and his friend, who agreed to come to this war without picking up a single weapon. Back in the Udyoga days, Arjuna chose Krishna that way, unarmed. Now the choice pays off in a way no one planned. Session three of six: the moment a soldier becomes a student.
screen: `A CHARIOT BETWEEN TWO ARMIES` → `THE DRIVER CARRIES NO WEAPON` → `A SOLDIER BECOMES A STUDENT`

segments.voice: At the start of the Gita's second chapter, Krishna first tries a soldier's language. Shake off this weakness. Stand up. It doesn't work. Arjuna answers with questions. How can he shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, men he should honor? Better to live as a beggar. Then he says the line that changes everything: I am your disciple. Teach me. I've come to you for refuge. He says he will not fight, and falls silent. And Krishna, as if smiling, there between the two armies, begins. You grieve for those you shouldn't grieve for. There was never a time when I was not, nor you, nor these kings, and there will never be a time when we cease to be. The self in each of them is never born and never dies. Weapons can't cut it. Fire can't burn it. The body is set aside the way a person puts away worn clothes and takes up new ones. This is one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the atman, the true self, eternal, behind every face. It's why Hindus speak of rebirth, the self taking up a new body the way you take up new clothes. And it's why, when someone dies, many Hindu families read from the Gita, often these very verses, at the bedside or at the prayer gathering. Read in place, it isn't a seminar on the soul. It's an answer to one grieving man about real people across the field: his grandfather, his teacher, his kin.
screen: `STAND UP: A SOLDIER'S WORDS FAIL` · `I AM YOUR DISCIPLE. TEACH ME.` · `THE BODY, LIKE WORN CLOTHES` · then, large: `ATMAN: NEVER BORN, NEVER DIES`

segments.voice: Many Hindus recite or listen to these verses for someone they've lost. Bring to mind someone you love who has died, or someone you're afraid of losing. Breathing in, picture their face. Breathing out, hold Krishna's words gently: what was truly them was never born and never dies. If you pray, you can place them in God's keeping. If you don't, simply hold them in mind with love.
Bhishma Parva. The book of the battle where, before a single arrow flies, a soldier asks to be taught, and hears that the self can never be killed.
Your line: the atman is never born and never dies. The great archer asked to be taught, and that was the first lesson. Day eight hundred twenty-one, done.

822.title: Work as an offering
822.hook: Arjuna pushes back on his teacher twice, and gets two great teachings: karma yoga, and God coming age after age.
822.carry: karma yoga: work as an offering, not for the prize
822.howItsDone: The Gita's third chapter is traditionally titled Karma Yoga, the yoga of action, and many Hindus close a task or a puja with 'Krishnarpanam astu', let this be offered to Krishna.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna said, the atman is never born and never dies. Your line: the atman is never born and never dies. Today the student pushes back.

Families have a way of keeping each other honest. Tell a story about yourself at a holiday dinner, and someone who grew up with you will say: that's not how it happened. Something like that happens in the middle of the Gita. Krishna mentions, almost in passing, that he taught this same teaching long ago, to the sun. And Arjuna, his cousin, stops him. Wait. Your birth came later. The sun was born long before you. How could you have taught him? Session four of six: the argument in the chariot.
screen: `FAMILY KEEPS YOU HONEST` → `I TAUGHT THIS TO THE SUN` → `WAIT: YOU WERE BORN AFTER HIM`

segments.voice: Read in place, Arjuna is not a polite student. At the start of the third chapter he says, more or less: if understanding is better than action, why push me into this terrible action? You're confusing me. Tell me one thing for certain. Krishna doesn't send him off to a cave. No one can stay free of action, he says, even for a moment. So act, but don't act for the prize. Act as an offering. He points to King Janaka, who reached the goal through action. Then a line that cuts close: better your own duty, done imperfectly, than someone else's done well. Hindus call this teaching karma yoga, the path of action. Your work, done fully and offered to God, becomes worship, and the result is left in God's hands. Krishna had already said it in the chapter before: your right is to the work, never to its fruits. That doesn't mean don't try. It means don't let the prize own you. Then the fourth chapter, and the moment from the hook. When Arjuna objects that Krishna was born after the sun, Krishna says: many births have passed for both of us. I know them all, and you don't. Whenever dharma fails, I come, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma right. The cousin in the driver's seat is beginning to show who he is. And it happens because Arjuna argued.
screen: `WHY PUSH ME INTO THIS ACTION?` · `NO ONE CAN STAY FREE OF ACTION` · `KARMA YOGA: WORK AS AN OFFERING` · then, large: `AGE AFTER AGE, I COME`

segments.voice: Many Hindus close a task or a prayer with the words Krishnarpanam astu: let this be offered to Krishna. Let your hands rest open and think of one ordinary task waiting for you. Breathing in, see yourself doing it fully. Breathing out, offer how it turns out: the praise, the grade, whether anyone notices. If you pray, you can say those words, or your own. If you don't, simply let the result go.

823.title: The universal form
823.hook: Arjuna is given a divine eye to see Krishna's universal form, and among the faces rushing into it are names the blind king knows.
823.carry: god is everything, yet comes as a friend
823.howItsDone: The vision of the universal form, the vishvarupa, in the Gita's eleventh chapter is read and recited, and appears in temple art and posters showing Krishna with many faces and arms before Arjuna's chariot, beside the gentler forms most homes keep on the shrine.

segments.voice: Yesterday Arjuna argued, and Krishna answered with karma yoga and a promise to come age after age. Your line: karma yoga: work as an offering, not for the prize.

Two people in this story are given eyes they weren't born with. One is Sanjaya, who sees the whole battlefield from the palace so he can tell the king. The other is Arjuna, who in the eleventh chapter of the Gita asks to see Krishna as he truly is, and is told his ordinary eyes can't do it. So Krishna gives him a divine eye. And then there's us, listening, because the one describing Arjuna's vision is Sanjaya, speaking to a blind father. Session five of six: the vision, heard from inside the palace.
screen: `EYES THEY WEREN'T BORN WITH` → `ARJUNA GETS A DIVINE EYE` → `SANJAYA TELLS THE BLIND KING`

segments.voice: Arjuna sees a form with countless faces and eyes, a light like a thousand suns rising at once, the whole universe gathered in one body. And remember who's telling it: Sanjaya, to a blind father. Then the vision turns. Arjuna sees the warriors rushing into terrible mouths, like rivers racing to the sea, like moths into a flame. The sons of Dhritarashtra. Bhishma. Drona. Karna. Our own warriors too. The blind king hears his own sons among them. Arjuna, shaking, asks: who are you? Krishna answers: I am Time, grown mighty, the destroyer of worlds. Be only the instrument. At the end, terrified, Arjuna asks to see his friend's familiar face again. Krishna takes his gentle form, and Arjuna says: now I'm myself again. Krishna adds that only loving devotion lets a person see him truly. Hindus call this vision the vishvarupa, the universal form: God as the whole universe, the light and the life, even time and death. And yet the same God comes back as a friend with a face. Here's the big teaching. Many Hindus worship one infinite God through forms they can love: a murti on the home shrine, baby Krishna with butter on his hands, the charioteer at the reins. Many teachers read this chapter as the reason. The infinite is real, and too much to hold. The familiar face isn't a smaller god. It's the door.
screen: `A THOUSAND SUNS AT ONCE` · `I AM TIME. BE THE INSTRUMENT.` · `THE FAMILIAR FACE AGAIN` · then, large: `VISHVARUPA: GOD AS EVERYTHING`

segments.voice: Many Hindus keep a small murti or picture of God at home. Let your gaze go soft and widen your attention: the room, the street, the sky over it, everything at once. Then come back, gently, to one familiar thing: the picture on your shrine if you have one, or a cup, or your own hand. Stay there. If you pray, let that familiar face be your door to the infinite. If you don't, notice how the near thing steadies you.
Bhishma Parva. The book whose grandsire stands in the ranks while Arjuna's vision of everything names him among those Time has already taken.

The teaching ends. Arjuna tells Krishna his confusion is gone and he will do as Krishna says. He picks up his bow. Both armies roar. And then, before a single arrow flies, Yudhishthira does something strange. He takes off his armor. He lays down his weapons. He climbs out of his chariot and walks, on foot, straight toward the enemy lines. His brothers run after him, asking where he's going. The other army starts to murmur that he's come to surrender. Session six of six: what the Gita leads into.
screen: `ARJUNA PICKS UP HIS BOW` → `YUDHISHTHIRA TAKES OFF HIS ARMOR` → `WALKING TOWARD THE ENEMY`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira walks to Bhishma, bows to him, and asks his permission to fight him, and his blessing. Bhishma is moved. In Ganguli's telling, he says that if Yudhishthira had not come to him like this, he would have cursed him with defeat. Instead he blesses him: fight, and win. Then he says something painfully honest about himself. A person is a slave to wealth, but wealth is no one's slave. I am bound to the Kauravas by their wealth. Ask me for anything except to fight on your side. So Yudhishthira asks a harder question. How can you be beaten? No one can defeat me now, Bhishma tells him, and the time of my death has not yet come. Ask me again another time. Yudhishthira goes on to his teachers, Drona and Kripa, and to his uncle Shalya, and does the same with each. And when he calls out for anyone who would choose his side, one of Dhritarashtra's own sons, Yuyutsu, crosses over. Here is something Hindu families still live by: ashirvad, the blessing of elders. Before a wedding, an exam or a journey, you bow to your elders, often touching their feet, and ask for their blessing. Being on opposite sides doesn't cancel the bond. Yudhishthira is about to fight these men, and he won't begin without honoring them. And they bless him, even Bhishma, who leads the other army. Many teachers read it this way: respect isn't the same as agreement, and it doesn't wait until you agree.

825.title: Bhishma's terrible vow
825.hook: the Kaurava commander loves the men he is fighting, and the reason he's there at all is a vow he made as a young prince.
825.carry: bhishma pratigya: a vow that binds for life
825.howItsDone: Bhishma's vow and the boon that lets him choose his death are told in the Mahabharata's Adi book, and 'Bhishma pratigya' is still used in Hindi for an unbreakable vow.

segments.voice: Yesterday Yudhishthira walked unarmed to Bhishma for his ashirvad, his blessing, and the grandsire gave it. Your line: ashirvad: honor your elders, even across the field.

An army might want a commander who hates the enemy. Duryodhana's commander doesn't. When Duryodhana asked Bhishma to lead his forces, in the Udyoga book, the old man said yes, and then set terms. The sons of Pandu, he said, are as dear to me as you are. I will fight their armies for you. I will not kill them. And there was a second problem, standing right there in the hall: Karna. Today, Bhishma's fall begins, with the strange shape of the side he leads.
screen: `A COMMANDER WHO DOESN'T HATE` → `HIS TERMS: NOT THE FIVE BROTHERS` → `AND KARNA IN THE HALL`

segments.voice: Start with Karna. When Bhishma ranks the warriors on his own side, he rates Karna low, and Karna is stung. So Karna makes a vow of his own: as long as Bhishma lives, he will not fight. Now go back to his youth. Bhishma was born Devavrata, a prince and heir to the throne. When his father, King Shantanu, fell in love with Satyavati, her father wanted her sons to rule. So the young prince gave up the throne, and then, so that no child of his could ever claim it, swore never to marry. The epic says flowers rained from the sky, and he was called Bhishma: the one of the terrible vow. His father gave him a gift in return: death would not take him until he chose it. That vow is why he's here, bound to the throne he gave away, leading an army against grandsons he loves. In Hindi, an unbreakable promise is still called a Bhishma pratigya, a vow like Bhishma's. Hindus prize a vow kept, and many keep vows of their own, vrats of fasting or prayer on certain days. But the epic doesn't make it simple. Many readers see Bhishma's vow as both his greatness and his tragedy: a promise made out of love that now binds him to the wrong side. On the first day, Virata's sons Uttara and Shveta fall, Shveta at Bhishma's own hand. So how do you bring down a man who can't be beaten, and who chooses when he dies?
screen: `KARNA WON'T FIGHT WHILE BHISHMA LIVES` · `DEVAVRATA GIVES UP THE THRONE` · `THE BOON: DEATH WHEN HE CHOOSES` · then, large: `BHISHMA PRATIGYA: THE TERRIBLE VOW`

Breathing out, ask yourself quietly whether it still serves what's good, the question Bhishma's story leaves us with. If you pray, bring that promise into your prayer. If you don't, simply hold it up to the light.
Bhishma's fall. Not yet. Today it's a riddle: a commander bound by his own vow, who will die only when he chooses.

826.title: Krishna runs at Bhishma
826.hook: Krishna promised not to fight. Then he jumps down from the chariot and runs at Bhishma, and Bhishma welcomes him.
826.carry: bhakta vatsala: god bends for his devotees
826.howItsDone: The scene of Krishna leaping from the chariot toward Bhishma is told in the Bhishma book of the Mahabharata, remembered in Bhishma's dying praise in the Bhagavata Purana, and loved by devotees as a picture of Krishna as bhakta vatsala.

segments.voice: Yesterday we learned why Bhishma is here at all: the Bhishma pratigya, the vow he swore as a young prince. Your line: bhishma pratigya: a vow that binds for life.

A charioteer's work is the reins. Krishna came to this war with one promise: he would not take up a weapon. He drives the chariot, he talks, and in the Gita he taught. But he doesn't fight. Then, early in the battle, Bhishma is cutting through the Pandava ranks, and Arjuna is holding back. And Krishna leaps down from the chariot and runs at Bhishma on foot. Today: the day the driver breaks his word, and the man he runs at welcomes him.
screen: `KRISHNA CAME UNARMED` → `ARJUNA HOLDS BACK` → `THE DRIVER JUMPS DOWN`

segments.voice: Duryodhana has accused Bhishma of going easy on the Pandavas, and the old man is stung. So he fights like fire. And Arjuna, facing the grandfather he grew up with, fights gently; he can't make himself strike hard. Krishna sees the Pandava army breaking. He drops the reins, jumps down, and rushes at Bhishma with his discus raised. Bhishma doesn't flinch. He stands his ground, bow in hand, and calls out a welcome. Come, strike me down. To be killed by you would be an honor. Then Arjuna jumps down after Krishna, grabs him, and holds on, dragged along the ground until Krishna stops. Arjuna swears he'll fight in earnest, and Krishna climbs back into the chariot. Days later, it happens again, this time with nothing in Krishna's hand but his horse whip. Bhishma welcomes him again. Arjuna pulls him back again. Now hear why devotees love this scene. Krishna is called bhakta vatsala: tender toward his devotees. Many teachers read the charge this way: God would rather bend his own word than watch the people who love him fall. And look at Bhishma. In the Bhagavata Purana, as he lies dying, his last praise of Krishna remembers this very moment: Krishna, he says, set aside his own promise to make Bhishma's promise come true. The enemy commander is a devotee too. In Hindu bhakti, devotion, love runs both ways, and it can find you even on a battlefield.
